notes.text: Exceeding great — The greatest city of the known world at that day, it was then in its flourishing state greater than Babylon, whose compass was three hundred eighty-five furlongs, but Nineveh was in compass, four hundred and eighty. It is said, her walls were an hundred foot in height, her walls broad enough for three coaches to meet, and safely pass by each other; that it had fifteen hundred towers on its walls, each two hundred foot high, and one million, four hundred thousand men employed for eight years to build it. Of three days journey - To walk round the walls, allowing twenty miles to each day's journey.
Shall be overthrown — The threat is express. But there was a reserve with God, on condition of repentance.
From the greatest — Great and small, rich and poor.
Vanity — Vain, and helpless creatures. A lie - They promise much, but generally deceive those who trust in them.
Vain — Feeding yourselves with vain hopes of felicity, from those riches which you take from others by violence.

Spoken — Frequently, both immediately as at Sinai, and by his holy prophets, from time to time. That - That power is God's prerogative; and consequently all creatures, either against or without him, are poor impotent things.

Therefore — God is almighty, therefore he can easily destroy all his enemies: he is also merciful, and therefore will pardon good mens failings. Renderest - And this as he is obliged to do by his holy nature, so is he able to do it, being omnipotent, and willing to do it to the godly (which was the only thing that might be doubted, because of their manifold miscarriages) because he is merciful and gracious. David's desire and esteem of God, ver. 1-4. His satisfaction, and communion with God, ver. 5, 6. His joyful dependence upon God, ver. 7, 8. His holy triumph in him, ver. 9-12. A psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Judah.

glossa.text: *But yet to God,* etc. ((CASS.)) Diapsalma. Again he exhorts himself, that is, his own soul, to be made subject, and admonishes the rest. *My soul is subject.* This petition fixes strength in our mind.
*In God is my salvation. ((Ibid.))* Then safe and glorious in him: but now what? He himself is the God of my help.

*Hope ye. ((Ibid.))* His own faith being published abroad, he admonishes all who labour under superstitions to hope in the Lord. *Pour out.* ((AUG.)) Through tears the heart is poured out, etc., *as far as:* Whence, *Prick the eye, and it produces a tear; prick the heart, and it produces knowledge ((Eccl. XXII))*. *Hearts,* etc., evil thoughts.

*But yet vain. ((HIER.))* Or, join it thus, God is our helper; and although he so works with us, yet the sons of Adam are vain and lying in the balance, perverting the Scriptures, by which they may prove false things. ((CASS.)) Diapsalmus. He reproaches those who go astray, and admonishes them to trust in God, not in things that perish, which is what the psalm intends. *Lying in the balances.* Who with unjust weights deceive buyers, or wish to seem just, though they are deceitful. *In the balances.* In the scale of justice, whereby they deceive the more easily. *Unto the same thing,* whereby they may be believed fair.

*Hope ye not in.* ((AUG.)) As if he should say: Neither hope ye, nor desire ye, the things which, when gathered, are snatched away by others. *Do not,* thirsting he turns himself to them. *Do not. Rapines.* The prey which thou wilt seize is in a trap, thou holdest and art held; thou holdest, another's goods that is, and art held by the devil. O ruinous gains! thou findest money, thou losest justice. *Let them abound. Set not your heart.* ((CASS.)) He does not say: Do not possess, for he does not condemn riches, whereby we purchase heaven; but the heart set upon them, which does not spend but hoards.

*He hath spoken once.* ((AUG.)) *Set not your heart upon them.* Why? Because the *power* of judging belongs to the Son of God, etc., *as far as* nor let mercy be despaired of on account of that power. *Power belongeth to God:* there is no power to any man save from God who is just, although his equity lie hidden from thee.

notes.text: But this I say, brethren -- with great confidence. The time of our abode here is short. It plainly follows, that even they who have wives be as serious, zealous, active, dead to the world, as devoted to God, as holy in all manner of conversation, as if they had none — By so easy a transition does the apostle slide from every thing else to the one thing needful; and, forgetting whatever is temporal, is swallowed up in eternity.

And they that weep, as if they wept not — "Though sorrowful, yet always rejoicing." They that rejoice, as if they rejoiced not - Tempering their joy with godly fear. They that buy, as if they possessed not - Knowing themselves to be only stewards, not proprietors.

And they that use this world, as not abusing it — Not seeking happiness in it, but in God: using every thing therein only in such a manner and degree as most tends to the knowledge and love of God. For the whole scheme and fashion of this world - This marrying, weeping, rejoicing, and all the rest, not only will pass, but now passeth away, is this moment flying off like a shadow.

glossa.text: *This therefore I say.* Here he admonishes to temperance, as if he were to say: When you are joined together, that it may be done without sin; this counsel I give you, that they who have wives *be as though they had none.* This he does who, having a wife, renders the debt and does not exact it; who takes a wife on account of his own weakness, lamenting rather that he could not be without a wife than rejoicing that he has taken one, and most of all because they keep continence by equal consent. Those marriages surely are to be judged more blessed which, whether children have been begotten or offspring despised, have been able to keep continence by equal consent.

notes.text: The time is fulfilled — The time of my kingdom, foretold by Daniel, expected by you, is fully come.
Straightway leaving their nets, they followed him — From this time they forsook their employ, and constantly attended him. Happy they who follow Christ at the first call!

glossa.text:
*But after that. ((ISID.))* We have received grace for grace, things carnal are beheaded, things spiritual are quickened. The shadow ceasing, the truth is at hand. John in prison, the law in Judaea, Jesus in Galilee, salvation among the Gentiles.

*Preaching,* etc. *((HIER.)) Blessed are the poor in spirit, for they shall possess ((Matth. V))*, etc. To the earthly kingdom succeeds poverty, and to the poverty of Christians an everlasting kingdom; whence: *My kingdom is not of this world ((Joan. XVIII))*: for every earthly honour is froth, smoke, a dream.

*Repent ye. ((HIER.))* The sweetness of the fruit makes up for the bitterness of the root: the hope of the harbour delights away the perils of the sea, the hope of health softens the pain of the medicine. He who desires the kernel, let him break the nut: let him do penance who wishes to cleave to the eternal good. They can tell forth the praises of Christ who have deserved to come to the palm of pardon. Whence after penance preachers are chosen.

*He saw Simon. ((HIER.))* Simon, *obedient;* Andrew, *manly;* James, *supplanter;* John, *grace.* By these names, etc., *as far as* by prudence we obey, by justice we act manfully, by temperance we tread upon serpents, by fortitude we merit the grace of God.

((ID.)) Whom does worldly eloquence not intoxicate? With difficulty do men that are powerful, and noble, and rich, and with much more difficulty than these the eloquent, believe God. Their mind is blinded by riches and wealth and luxury, and, encompassed about with vices, they cannot see the virtues, and they judge the simplicity of Holy Scripture not from the majesty of its meanings, but from the serviceableness of its words.

((ID.)) Four fishermen are called, Simon, Andrew, James and John: leaving all things they follow. By this chariot we are borne to the upper air, etc., *as far as* we are covered with the skins of Solomon, in which the bride glories that she is beautiful.

((BEDA.)) It is asked how he called first Peter and Andrew, and after a little James and John, as he relates, etc., *as far as* for then they followed him, not with the ships drawn up to land as though with a care of returning, but as one calling and commanding.

*And they enter in. ((HIER.))* Mark, disposing the sayings of the Gospel within himself, not following the order of the history, keeps the order of the mysteries, whence on the sabbath he relates the first miracle, saying: *And they enter in,* etc.

*Capharnaum. ((ID.))* Capharnaum is the village of consolation, the sabbath is rest. The man in an unclean spirit, the human race, in which is uncleanness, etc., *as far as* Pharao, let go by Israel, we pursue him, the devil, despised, rises up into scandals.

((BEDA.)) That he heals and teaches chiefly on the sabbath shows that he is not under the law, but above it: and he teaches us the true sabbath, that, being zealous namely for the salvation of souls, we may abstain from every servile work, that is, from all unlawful things.

places.name: Nineveh
places.id: On the eastern bank of the Tigris opposite modern Mosul, Iraq. The two principal mounds are Tell Kuyunjik (the citadel and palaces of Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal) and Tell Nebi Yunus (traditionally Jonah's tomb, lower city). Excavated in the 1840s by Botta and Layard, who recovered the royal libraries and palace reliefs. The 'great city' of the book; capital of the Assyrian empire from Sennacherib's reign (c. 700 B.C.).

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: One generation goes, and another generation comes; but the earth remains forever.
echoes.note: Paul's declaration that 'the mode of this world passes away' and his counsel to hold possessions loosely echo Qoheleth's vision of generations and the world in ceaseless passing under the sun, where buying, weeping, and rejoicing are all hevel. Coherence is high: the 'as though not' detachment from marriage, mourning, joy, and commerce mirrors Ecclesiastes' relativizing of all worldly engagements. Volume is thematic; medium.

echoes.text: The voice of one saying, “Cry!” One said, “What shall I cry?” “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, because Yahweh’s breath blows on it. Surely the people are like grass. The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”
echoes.note: Paul's claim that 'the present form of this world is passing away' stands in the prophetic tradition of Isa 40:6-8, where 'all flesh is grass' and the world's glory withers while God's word stands—the contrast of transient world and enduring divine order that grounds Paul's eschatological detachment. Coherence and availability are high. Volume conceptual; medium confidence.

echoes.text: Behold, you have made my days hand breadths. My lifetime is as nothing before you. Surely every man stands as a breath.” Selah. “Surely every man walks like a shadow. Surely they busy themselves in vain. He heaps up, and doesn’t know who shall gather.
echoes.note: Paul's 'those who buy as though they did not possess' and the fleeting 'form of this world' closely match Ps 39:6: 'man goes about as a shadow; he heaps up wealth and does not know who will gather it.' The shared image of buying/possessing as vain because life and world are transient is distinctive. Coherence with Paul's 'as though not' is strong; medium.

echoes.text: Be silent at the presence of the Lord Yahweh, for the day of Yahweh is at hand. For Yahweh has prepared a sacrifice. He has consecrated his guests.
echoes.note: Paul's sense that 'the time has grown short' and 'distress is upon us' echoes the prophetic announcement that the Day of the Lord is near and at hand (Zeph 1:7, 14), with its imminence relativizing ordinary life and commerce. Availability is secure; volume is low and the imminence motif is widespread, so the specific echo is contested.

echoes.text: a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
echoes.note: Paul's catalogue 'those who weep as though they did not weep, those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice' faintly recalls Qoheleth's 'a time to weep and a time to laugh,' the sapiential relativizing of the emotional seasons of life. The link is thematic and the wording diverges; faint and contested.

echoes.text: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.
echoes.note: Paul's reference to the present 'distress' and the foreshortened time may draw on Danielic expectation of a time of unparalleled distress before the end (Dan 12:1) and the apocalyptic notion of an appointed time cut short. Availability is good in a Second-Temple frame; volume is low and generic, so this is a faint contested echo.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: 'The kingdom of God is at hand' announced as 'good news' fulfills the herald of Isaiah 52:7 who proclaims good news and says 'Your God reigns.' Volume couples the distinctive verb euangelizō with the reign of God, both present here; recurrence binds it to 1:1's euangelion. Coherence is maximal—this is Mark's thesis statement drawn from Isaiah's gospel of God's kingship.

echoes.text: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.
echoes.note: The expectation that 'the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed' supplies the apocalyptic content of Jesus' 'kingdom of God.' Volume is conceptual but the specific phrase 'kingdom of God/heaven' has its clearest Second-Temple anchor in Daniel; coherence with Mark's 'the time is fulfilled' (an apocalyptic timetable) is strong.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The everlasting dominion given to the 'one like a son of man' is the kingdom Mark's Jesus proclaims and later claims (Mark 13:26; 14:62). In 1:15 the contact is thematic—the inbreaking eternal kingdom—rather than verbal, but the recurrence of Daniel 7 across Mark gives the echo real weight here.

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound; to proclaim the year of Yahweh’s favor, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all who mourn;
echoes.note: 'The time is fulfilled' resonates with Isaiah 61:2's 'the acceptable year of the LORD,' the proclamation of the eschatological jubilee by the Spirit-anointed herald (cf. Jesus' anointing at 1:10). Volume is moderate on the 'favorable/fulfilled time' motif; coherence with the gospel-of-God framing is good, though Mark does not quote it as Luke does.
echoes.lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind; to declare the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of recompence; to comfort all that mourn;

echoes.text: Your doom has come to you, inhabitant of the land: the time has come, the day is near, a day of tumult, and not of joyful shouting, on the mountains.
echoes.note: Ezekiel 7:7,12 declare 'the time has come, the day is near,' a near-formula for Mark's 'the time is fulfilled.' Volume is the shared 'the time has come' idiom, but Ezekiel's announcement is judgment, not gospel, weakening coherence; included as a faint, contested verbal parallel.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send for many fishermen, says Yahweh, and they shall fish them up; and afterward I will send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain, and from every hill, and out of the clefts of the rocks.
echoes.note: 'I will make you into fishers for men' draws on Jeremiah 16:16, 'I will send for many fishers... and they shall fish them.' Volume rests on the distinctive 'fishers of men' image, which is rare in scripture; coherence is the chief question because Jeremiah's fishers gather for judgment while Jesus' gather for salvation, a deliberate transvaluation. Distinctiveness makes the allusion likely.

echoes.text: So he departed there, and found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing, with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he with the twelfth: and Elijah passed over to him, and cast his mantle on him. He left the oxen, and ran after Elijah, and said, “Let me please kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you.” He said to him, “Go back again; for what have I done to you?” He returned from following him, and took the yoke of oxen, and killed them, […]
echoes.note: The abrupt prophetic call—Jesus passing by, the brothers immediately leaving father and livelihood—mirrors Elijah's call of Elisha, who left his oxen and his father to follow. Volume lies in the shared call-narrative form (summons in the midst of work, leaving family/trade), and Mark's pervasive Elijah typology raises coherence and recurrence for the pattern, even without direct quotation.

echoes.text: It shall happen, that fishermen shall stand by it: from En Gedi even to En Eglaim shall be a place for the spreading of nets; their fish shall be after their kinds, as the fish of the great sea, exceeding many.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's vision of fishermen spreading nets along the life-giving temple river offers a more positive 'fishers' background than Jeremiah's judgment. Volume is low (no verbal contact beyond 'fishermen/nets') and the link is thematic, so it is a contested alternate backdrop to the call of the fishermen.

echoes.text: The Lord Yahweh has sworn by his holiness that behold, “The days shall come on you that they will take you away with hooks, and the last of you with fish hooks.
echoes.note: Amos 4:2 threatens that the people will be taken away 'with fishhooks,' another OT fishing-for-people image. Volume is faint and, like Jeremiah, the valence is judgment; included for maximal coverage of the 'catching people' metaphor though coherence with Jesus' summons is weak.

registers.label: Spare
lines: The time is fulfilled; the kingdom of God is near.
Repent, and believe the good news.
Jesus walked the shore and called the fishermen.
Follow me, and I will make you fish for people.
They left their nets and went with him.
Here we are; we leave our nets to follow.
Come, let us worship and answer the call.
Here we are; we follow you. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Down by the sea the nets were heavy and wet, the morning's work half done, when a stranger walked the shore and called them by name.
We leave our nets and follow you.
The time is fulfilled, he said, the kingdom of God has come near; turn around, and trust the good news.
We leave our nets and follow you.
And they left the boats, left the nets, left their father with the hired hands, and went.
We leave our nets and follow you.
For God alone our souls wait in silence; he is our rock, and when he calls we rise.
We leave our nets and follow you. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Jesus walks the shore where the nets are drying.
We leave our nets and follow you.
The kingdom is near; repent and believe.
We leave our nets and follow you.
They drop the nets and leave the boat behind.
We leave our nets and follow you.
Come, let us worship and answer his call.
We leave our nets and follow you. Amen.
